chapters.title: Queens
paragraphs: Donald John Trump was born on June 14, 1946, in Queens, New York City, the fourth of five children. His father, Fred Trump, built and rented apartments in the outer boroughs. His mother, Mary Anne MacLeod Trump, had come from Scotland. The family lived in Jamaica Estates, and Donald learned the business working for his father.

At 13 his parents sent him to the New York Military Academy, a private boarding school. He spent two years at Fordham, then transferred to the University of Pennsylvania. In 1968 he finished a bachelor’s degree in economics at the Wharton School and went into the family company.

sources.label: Miller Center · Life before the presidency

chapters.title: Manhattan, and the name on the building
paragraphs: He took charge of the family company in the early 1970s and went after projects in Manhattan. With Hyatt, he rebuilt the run-down Commodore Hotel near Grand Central, using a city tax deal. The Grand Hyatt opened in 1980. Trump Tower, on Fifth Avenue, opened in 1983. It became his home and the company’s headquarters.

In 1973 the Justice Department sued Donald Trump, his father, and their company, alleging racial discrimination in apartment rentals under the Fair Housing Act. They disputed the allegations. A 1975 consent decree imposed fair-housing rules and included no admission of liability.

He bought Mar-a-Lago in 1985 and later turned it into a private club. He also moved into Atlantic City casinos, including the Trump Taj Mahal. The borrowing was heavy. When the money coming in fell short, the business was exposed. Casino companies went into corporate bankruptcy, and Trump shifted more of the work toward licensing his name.

sources.label: University of Michigan · Fair Housing Act case and original filings

chapters.title: Family, and the television years
paragraphs: He married Ivana Zelníčková in 1977. They had Donald Jr., Ivanka and Eric, and divorced in 1992. He married Marla Maples in 1993, the year their daughter Tiffany was born, and they divorced in 1999. In 2005 he married Melania Knauss, a model born in Slovenia. Their son Barron was born in 2006. During his first time in the White House, Ivanka and her husband Jared Kushner worked as advisers.

The Art of the Deal, the 1987 book he wrote with Tony Schwartz, presented him as a dealmaker. He later owned beauty pageants and put his name on hotels, golf courses and ordinary consumer products. From 2004, NBC’s The Apprentice, and later The Celebrity Apprentice, put that boardroom version of him in front of a national audience. A lot of voters already felt they knew him.

chapters.title: The first win
paragraphs: He made a brief run for the Reform Party nomination in 2000. He drew political attention again in 2011 by promoting the false claim that Barack Obama had been born outside the United States. In June 2015 he launched a Republican campaign at Trump Tower. Border restrictions, trade, and the line “Make America Great Again” were the heart of the pitch.

He won the Republican nomination and chose Indiana governor Mike Pence as his running mate. On November 8, 2016, he beat Hillary Clinton. She won more votes nationwide. He won the states that decided it, and took 304 electoral votes to her 227. He entered office without having held a government or military job.

chapters.title: The first term
paragraphs: The 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act lowered the corporate income-tax rate and changed individual taxes. The administration restricted entry from several countries and pushed for a border wall. In 2018 its zero-tolerance prosecutions separated thousands of migrant children from their parents. His Supreme Court nominees, Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett, were all confirmed.

He took the United States out of the Iran nuclear deal, put tariffs on Chinese imports, and replaced NAFTA with the United States–Mexico–Canada Agreement. He recognized Jerusalem as Israel’s capital and moved the embassy there. The Abraham Accords, in 2020, established formal relations between Israel and the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain. Other normalization agreements followed.

The administration also withdrew from the Paris climate agreement. That decision took effect in November 2020. In June 2018 he met Kim Jong Un in Singapore, the first meeting between a sitting U.S. president and a North Korean leader. They issued a statement saying they would work toward denuclearizing the Korean Peninsula.

COVID-19 took over the last year. He signed the CARES Act and launched Operation Warp Speed to speed up vaccine development and purchasing. The first vaccines received U.S. emergency authorization in December 2020. He also kept playing the threat down, and he clashed in public with health officials.

sources.label: White House archive · Singapore summit statement

chapters.title: Russia, Ukraine, January 6
paragraphs: Special Counsel Robert Mueller documented Russian interference in the 2016 election. The investigation did not establish that the Trump campaign conspired or coordinated with the Russian government in that interference. Mueller also looked at possible obstruction, and he declined to make a normal prosecutorial judgment on that question.

In December 2019 the House impeached him for abuse of power and obstruction of Congress. He had pressed Ukraine’s president to announce investigations that could help him politically. Trump said the call was appropriate. The Senate acquitted him on both articles in February 2020.

Joe Biden won in 2020, 306 electoral votes to 232. Trump said, falsely, that widespread fraud had cost him the election, and he pressed officials to undo the result. On January 6, 2021, a mob attacked the Capitol and interrupted the count. Congress came back into session and certified Biden’s victory. The House impeached Trump for incitement of insurrection. In the Senate, 57 senators voted to convict and 43 to acquit, short of the two-thirds required.

chapters.title: The cases
paragraphs: A New York jury convicted him in May 2024 on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records, connected to reimbursements for a payment to Stormy Daniels before the 2016 election. He denied wrongdoing. An unconditional discharge in January 2025 left the conviction on the books, without a fine, probation or jail. A state appeals panel heard argument on November 5, 2026.

Two civil juries awarded E. Jean Carroll $5 million for sexual abuse and defamation, and $83.3 million in a separate defamation case. Trump denied her allegations. In another New York civil case, about inflated asset values, a state appeals court in 2025 left the liability findings in place and threw out the financial penalty.

Federal cases over the 2020 election and over classified documents ended without a trial for Trump. After he was reelected, prosecutors moved to dismiss the federal election case, citing Justice Department policy against prosecuting a sitting president. A federal judge had already dismissed the documents case, on grounds related to the special counsel’s appointment. Georgia’s separate 2020 election case was dismissed in November 2025, after a new prosecutor asked the court to drop it.

chapters.title: Back from Mar-a-Lago
paragraphs: Out of office, he stayed influential in the Republican Party. He endorsed candidates and used Truth Social to talk to supporters. He announced a third presidential campaign in November 2022, beat primary rivals including Ron DeSantis and Nikki Haley, and picked Ohio senator JD Vance as his running mate.

He survived an assassination attempt at a rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, in July 2024. That month Biden withdrew, and Vice President Kamala Harris became the Democratic nominee. Trump campaigned on inflation, immigration and tariffs. He beat Harris 312 to 226 in the Electoral College and took the oath on January 20, 2025, the first president since Grover Cleveland to serve terms that were not back to back.

sources.label: Miller Center · Life between the presidencies

chapters.title: The second term
paragraphs: He returned with a Republican Congress. On his first day he granted widespread clemency for January 6 offenses and signed an order meant to limit birthright citizenship. In July 2025 Congress passed a reconciliation bill that extended tax cuts, added funding for immigration enforcement, and changed Medicaid eligibility and work requirements.

The United States withdrew from the Paris Agreement again, effective January 2026. In February 2026 the Supreme Court ruled that the emergency-powers law he had cited did not authorize his broad tariffs. In June the Court held that the Constitution guarantees citizenship to children born in the United States whose parents are in the country unlawfully or only for a time. That blocked his effort to narrow the guarantee by executive order.

The United States and Israel launched strikes on Iran in February 2026. By mid-November there was still no lasting agreement. In the November midterms, Democrats won the incoming majorities in both chambers of Congress. Republican control of the whole government ends when the new Congress sits in January 2027.
